 The ballad stanzas of MA are consciously written in what Leigh Hunt describes in his
Preface of 1832 as ‘a lax and familiar measure’ and Mary in her ‘Note on Poems of 1819’
in 1839 considered as ‘a more popular tone than usual . . . portions strik[ing] as abrupt
and unpolished’. In a letter of mid-November 1819, S. reminds Hunt that ‘my lines on the
Manchester affair . . . are of the exoteric species’ — that is, aimed at a broad readership
encompassing those without the intellectual and literary sophistication demanded by his
more usual ‘esoteric’ verse — and so intended for the Examiner which, so he judged, would
